content: 1. Vaginal delivery is not recommended under certain conditions, based on very low-quality evidence. 2. Performing digital vaginal examinations every four hours is strongly recommended for routine assessment during the active first stage of labor in low-risk women, despite the evidence being of very low quality. 3. Routine vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine during labor to prevent infectious morbidities is not recommended, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 4. Routine vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine in women colonized with Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is not recommended for preventing early neonatal GBS infection, based on very low-quality evidence. 5. Administering intrapartum antibiotics to women colonized with GBS is conditionally recommended to prevent early neonatal GBS infection, despite the evidence being of very low quality. 6. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis during the second or third trimester for all women to reduce infectious morbidity is not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 7. Routine antibiotic administration is not recommended for women in preterm labor with intact amniotic membranes, based on moderate-quality evidence. 8. Antibiotic administration is strongly recommended for women with preterm prelabor rupture of membranes, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 9. Routine antibiotic administration is not recommended for women with prelabor rupture of membranes at or near term, based on low-quality evidence. 10. Routine antibiotic administration is not recommended for women with meconium-stained amniotic fluid, based on low-quality evidence. 11. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is strongly recommended for women undergoing manual removal of the placenta, despite the evidence being of very low quality. 12. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for women undergoing operative vaginal birth, based on very low-quality evidence. 13. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is strongly recommended for women with thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears, despite the evidence being of very low quality. 14. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for women with episiotomy, based on consensus views. 15. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for women with uncomplicated vaginal birth, supported by very low-quality evidence. 16. Vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine immediately before cesarean section is conditionally recommended, based on moderate-quality evidence. 17. The choice of antiseptic agent and method of application for skin preparation prior to cesarean section should be based on the clinician’s experience, cost, and local availability, supported by low-quality evidence. 18. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is strongly recommended for women undergoing elective or emergency cesarean section, based on moderate-quality evidence. 19. Prophylactic antibiotics for cesarean section should be administered prior to skin incision rather than intraoperatively after umbilical cord clamping, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 20. For antibiotic prophylaxis in cesarean section, a single dose of first-generation cephalosporin or penicillin is preferred over other antibiotic classes, based on very low-quality evidence. 21. Induction of labor is recommended for women who are confirmed to have reached 41 weeks of gestation, supported by low-quality evidence. 22. Induction of labor is not recommended for women with uncomplicated pregnancies at gestational ages less than 41 weeks, based on low-quality evidence. 23. Induction of labor before 41 weeks of gestation is not recommended if gestational diabetes is the only abnormality, supported by very low-quality evidence. 24. Induction of labor at term is not recommended for suspected fetal macrosomia, based on low-quality evidence. 25. Induction of labor is strongly recommended for women with prelabor rupture of membranes at term, supported by high-quality evidence. 26. If prostaglandins are unavailable, intravenous oxytocin alone should be used for induction of labor, but amniotomy alone is not recommended, based on moderate-quality evidence. 27. Oral misoprostol (25 µg every 2 hours) is strongly recommended for induction of labor, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 28. Low-dose vaginal misoprostol (25 µg every 6 hours) is strongly recommended for induction of labor, based on moderate-quality evidence. 29. Misoprostol is not recommended for induction of labor in women with a previous cesarean section, supported by low-quality evidence. 30. Low doses of vaginal prostaglandins are strongly recommended for induction of labor, based on moderate-quality evidence. 31. A balloon catheter is strongly recommended for induction of labor, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 32. The combination of a balloon catheter and oxytocin is recommended as an alternative method of induction of labor when prostaglandins are unavailable or contraindicated, based on low-quality evidence. 33. In the third trimester, oral or vaginal misoprostol is strongly recommended for induction of labor in women with a dead or anomalous fetus, supported by low-quality evidence. 34. Sweeping membranes is strongly recommended to reduce the need for formal induction of labor, based on moderate-quality evidence. 35. Betamimetics are weakly recommended for women experiencing uterine hyperstimulation during induction of labor, based on low-quality evidence. 36. Outpatient induction of labor is not recommended for improving birth outcomes, based on low-quality evidence. 37. Active phase partograph with a four-hour action line is strongly recommended for monitoring labor progress, supported by low-quality evidence. 38. Digital vaginal examination every four hours is weakly recommended for routine assessment and identification of delay in active labor, based on very low-quality evidence. 39. A package of care for active management of labor to prevent delay is not recommended, based on low-quality evidence. 40. Early amniotomy with early oxytocin augmentation to prevent delay in labor is not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 41. The use of oxytocin to prevent delay in labor in women receiving epidural analgesia is not recommended, based on low-quality evidence. 42. Amniotomy alone to prevent delay in labor is not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 43. The use of antispasmodic agents to prevent delay in labor is not recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 44. Pain relief to prevent delay and reduce the use of augmentation in labor is not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 45. The use of intravenous fluids to shorten labor duration is not recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 46. Oral fluid and food intake during labor is weakly recommended for low-risk women, supported by very low-quality evidence. 47. Encouraging mobility and upright positions during labor in low-risk women is strongly recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 48. Continuous companionship during labor is strongly recommended to improve labor outcomes, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 49. Administration of enemas to reduce the use of labor augmentation is not recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 50. The use of oxytocin alone for treating delay in labor is weakly recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 51. Augmentation with intravenous oxytocin before confirming delay in labor is not recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 52. High starting and increment dosage regimens of oxytocin for labor augmentation are not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 53. The use of oral misoprostol for labor augmentation is not recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 54. Amniotomy alone for treating delay in labor is not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 55. The use of amniotomy and oxytocin for treating confirmed delay in labor is weakly recommended, based on very low-quality evidence. 56. Internal tocodynamometry compared to external tocodynamometry for improving outcomes in augmented labor is not recommended, supported by very low-quality evidence. 57. The use of uterotonics during the third stage of labor to prevent postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is strongly recommended for all births, based on moderate-quality evidence. 58. Oxytocin (10 IU, IV/IM) is the recommended uterotonic drug for preventing PPH, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 59. In settings where oxytocin is unavailable, other injectable uterotonics (e.g., ergometrine/methylergometrine or a fixed drug combination of oxytocin and ergometrine) or oral misoprostol (600 µg) are strongly recommended, based on moderate-quality evidence. 60. In settings without skilled birth attendants and where oxytocin is unavailable, community or lay health workers administering misoprostol (600 µg PO) is strongly recommended for PPH prevention, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 61. In settings with skilled birth attendants, controlled cord traction (CCT) is weakly recommended for vaginal births if reducing blood loss and shortening the third stage of labor are considered important, based on high-quality evidence. 62. In settings without skilled birth attendants, CCT is not recommended, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 63. Late cord clamping (1–3 minutes after birth) is strongly recommended for all births while initiating essential newborn care, based on moderate-quality evidence. 64. Early cord clamping (<1 minute after birth) is not recommended unless the neonate is asphyxiated and requires immediate resuscitation, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 65. Sustained uterine massage is not recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH in women who have received prophylactic oxytocin, based on low-quality evidence. 66. Postpartum abdominal uterine tone assessment for early identification of uterine atony is strongly recommended for all women, supported by very low-quality evidence. 67. Oxytocin (IV or IM) is the recommended uterotonic drug for PPH prevention in cesarean sections, based on moderate-quality evidence. 68. Controlled cord traction (CCT) is the recommended method for placenta removal in cesarean sections, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 69. After an uncomplicated vaginal birth in a health facility, healthy mothers and newborns should remain in the facility for at least 24 hours, based on low-quality evidence. 70. If birth occurs at home, the first postnatal contact should occur as early as possible within 24 hours of birth. 71. At least three additional postnatal contacts are recommended for all mothers and newborns: on day 3 (48–72 hours), between days 7–14, and six weeks after birth. This is strongly recommended for newborns (moderate-quality evidence) and weakly recommended for mothers (low-quality evidence). 72. Home visits during the first week after birth are strongly recommended for the care of the mother and newborn, supported by low-to-moderate quality evidence. 73. All postpartum women should have regular assessments of vaginal bleeding, uterine contraction, fundal height, temperature, and heart rate during the first 24 hours, starting from the first hour after birth. Blood pressure should also be measured shortly after birth.
